raw_text:
### Introduction and Definitions
Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is a life-threatening, pregnancy-associated form of systolic heart failure that predominantly affects previously healthy young women [1]. Over the past two decades, consensus groups have refined the clinical definition of PPCM. In 2000, the National Institutes of Health (NIH) workshop established that PPCM is characterized by the development of heart failure in the last month of pregnancy or within five months postpartum, without an identifiable alternative cause or prior history of heart disease [2]. Subsequently, the Heart Failure Association (HFA) of the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) extended this definition by emphasizing left ventricular (LV) systolic dysfunction with a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) typically below 45% [3]. Because PPCM requires rapid recognition and collaborative treatment, current guidelines strongly advocate for a multidisciplinary "Pregnancy Heart Team" to coordinate maternal-fetal care [4].

### Epidemiology and Risk Factors
The incidence of PPCM varies considerably across geographic regions and ethnic populations. In the United States, epidemiological data indicate a steady increase in PPCM cases over the past several decades, now affecting approximately 1 in 1,000 to 4,000 live births [5]. There is a pronounced racial disparity in disease burden; Black women face a significantly higher risk of developing PPCM and experience higher rates of persistent myocardial dysfunction and mortality compared to other racial groups [6]. While PPCM can occur in any pregnancy, classic predisposing factors include advanced maternal age, multifetal gestation, multiparity, and chronic hypertension [7]. Indeed, global registry data confirm a high prevalence of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy among women diagnosed with PPCM [8]. A strong clinical and mechanistic association has been established with pre-eclampsia, which dramatically increases a patient’s susceptibility to acute myocardial failure [9].

### Pathophysiology and Genetics
The understanding of PPCM pathogenesis has transitioned from an idiopathic inflammatory state to a "two-hit" model characterized by vascular dysfunction and genetic susceptibility. During late pregnancy and the early postpartum period, elevated systemic oxidative stress activates the protease cathepsin D, which cleaves the nursing hormone prolactin into a vasculotoxic 16 kDa N-terminal fragment [10]. This 16 kDa prolactin fragment triggers endothelial cell apoptosis, disrupts capillary networks, and directly compromises cardiomyocyte metabolism [10]. This pro-apoptotic signaling is further exacerbated by systemic angiogenic imbalance. In late gestation, the placenta secretes high levels of soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt-1), a decoy receptor that neutralizes vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and impairs cardiac angiogenesis [11]. The combined anti-angiogenic stress of sFlt-1 and cleaved prolactin drives microvascular damage and heart failure [12]. Concurrently, genetic studies have revealed a substantial genetic overlap between PPCM and dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) [13]. Approximately 10% to 15% of women with PPCM harbor pathogenic variants in sarcomeric genes, most notably truncating mutations in the titin (*TTN*) gene [14]. This genetic predisposition appears to reduce sarcomeric compliance, rendering the maternal heart vulnerable to the physiological demands of gestation [15].

### Clinical Presentation and Diagnosis
The clinical presentation of PPCM spans from mild exertional dyspnea to severe acute pulmonary edema or cardiogenic shock [16]. Because symptoms of early heart failure (such as fatigue, peripheral edema, and orthopnea) mimic normal physiological changes of late pregnancy, diagnosis is frequently delayed [16]. Transthoracic echocardiography remains the primary diagnostic tool, allowing for the quantitative evaluation of biventricular size and systolic function [17]. Electrocardiography (ECG) is also standard; though non-specific, it frequently reveals sinus tachycardia, ST-T wave abnormalities, or prolongation of the corrected QT interval [18]. When diagnostic ambiguity persists or if precise tissue characterization is required, cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging can be utilized to evaluate myocardial edema, right ventricular involvement, and late gadolinium enhancement [19].

### Medical Management
The therapeutic management of PPCM must carefully balance maternal benefit with fetal safety. Prior to delivery, standard guideline-directed medical therapies (GDMT) such as angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs) are strictly contraindicated due to teratogenicity and fetotoxicity [20]. Consequently, antepartum management relies on loop diuretics, beta-blockers, and a combination of hydralazine and nitrates [20]. Following delivery, standard GDMT can be aggressively implemented [20]. 

In addition to standard heart failure therapies, suppressing prolactin secretion using bromocriptine has emerged as a disease-specific treatment [21]. A proof-of-concept pilot study showed that adding bromocriptine to standard therapy improved LVEF and survival [21]. This was validated in a larger, multicenter randomized controlled trial in Germany, demonstrating high rates of LVEF recovery with both short-term and long-term bromocriptine regimens [22]. Bromocriptine has also been shown to promote myocardial recovery in patients presenting with concomitant right ventricular dysfunction [23]. Comprehensive meta-analyses have reinforced these findings, suggesting that prolactin inhibition represents a safe and effective strategy for accelerating myocardial recovery [24]. Because prolactin inhibition and the peripartum state are highly prothrombotic, therapeutic or prophylactic anticoagulation must be co-administered with bromocriptine, particularly in patients with an LVEF below 30% [25].

### Prognosis and Subsequent Pregnancies
Myocardial recovery in PPCM is highly variable but generally superior to other forms of non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy. In North America, the Investigations of Pregnancy-Associated Cardiomyopathy (IPAC) study demonstrated that approximately 70% of women achieve myocardial recovery (LVEF ≥ 50%) within one year of diagnosis, though baseline LVEF < 30% and Black ancestry remain strong predictors of persistent dysfunction [26]. However, global registries highlight significant regional disparities, with lower recovery rates and higher mortality in developing countries [27]. For women contemplating a subsequent pregnancy, rigorous pre-pregnancy evaluation and counseling are mandatory [28]. The risk of heart failure recurrence remains high; while women with persistent LV dysfunction face a catastrophic risk of clinical deterioration, those with fully recovered LV function still harbor a 20% risk of relapse [29]. Continued research into biomarker profiles and genomic sequencing is crucial to individualizing risk stratification and optimizing long-term outcomes [30].
